In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out. As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity and dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever should not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children, is emphasized by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to deepen the provisions of articles 77 to article 90, which already provide quite severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this perda for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment

is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295 which is 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law is quite severe in establishing criminal threats and fines as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe punishment threats or sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so it is still far from reality, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the demands and verdicts of judges are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays KDRT is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of KDRT in Musi Rawas Regency at the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency, an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency has been established, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/ KPTS/ KPP/2015 namely

concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) becomes a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is KDRT or other violence that befalls women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, but the existence of P2TP2A is not widely known by the community.

In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out. As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to deepen the provisions of articles 77 to article 90, which already provide quite severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this perda for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295 which is 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law is quite severe in establishing criminal threats and fines as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe punishment threats or sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so it is still far from reality, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the demands and verdicts of judges are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays KDRT is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of KDRT in Musi Rawas Regency at the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency, an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency has been established, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/ KPTS/ KPP/2015 namely

concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) becomes a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is KDRT or other violence that befalls women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, but the existence of P2TP2A is not widely known by the community.

From the provisions of the legislation mentioned above, we can understand how great the attention of the Central Government is to protect its citizens who are in an unpleasant position, namely when becoming victims of violence, but in reality legal processes are still few that are carried out for victims of violence which are increasingly numerous and complex in their problems today. Types of KDRT, include:

Physical violence is any act that results in pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that results in fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse in an unnatural or unwanted manner, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women facing the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under 18 years of age, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in a direct line upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or stepfather and/or stepmother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises parental authority as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental obstacles that interfere with their growth and development naturally. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of the adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because their parents or one of their parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop children in accordance with their religion and abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Child's rights are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, society, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in conflict with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are economically and/or sexually exploited, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substance abuse (drugs), children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of mistreatment and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to the victim when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against the victim will, is, or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for strengthening and self-recovery of victims of violence. 33. Assistance is all actions in the form of counseling, psychological therapy, advocacy, and spiritual guidance, for strengthening victims of domestic violence to resolve the problems they face. 34. Integrated Service Center for Women and Children Empowerment (P2TP2A) hereinafter abbreviated as P2TP2A is an institution providing services to victims of violence, based in hospitals, managed jointly in the form of medical services (including medico-legal), psycho-social and legal services. 35. Cooperation is a systematic and integrated way among recovery implementers in providing services to recover victims of domestic violence. 36. Safe house is a temporary residence used to provide protection to victims in accordance with determined operational standards. 37.

Article 4

The purpose of establishing this Regional Regulation is to provide protection and services to women and children victims of violence based on gender and the best interests of the child occurring in the household and/or public. As well as to guarantee the fulfillment of children's rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination, for the realization of quality Indonesian children with noble character and prosperity.

The National Objective of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph states that it includes: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all of Indonesia's homeland, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to deepen the provisions of articles 77 to article 90, which already provide quite severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this perda for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

In order for us to better understand the prohibition of KDRT, a brief description of important matters from Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning KDRT will be outlined as follows:

Types of KDRT, include:

a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) falling ill, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of helplessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, who resides within the household, (2) forced sexual relations against one person within the household with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household, whereas according to the law applicable to him or because of an agreement or contract he is obliged to provide life, care, or

maintenance to that person or child, (2) resulting in economic dependence by limiting and/or prohibiting to work properly inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. The rights of KDRT victims are to obtain:

To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. PROTECTION OF WOMEN AND CHILDREN VICTIMS OF VIOLENCE

I. GENERAL

The National Objective of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph states that it includes: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all of Indonesia's homeland, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila, and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

The principles of this Perda are the principles contained in previous laws and regulations, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, is actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal rule on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government. Also in, Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially regulates that every person, of course both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the right of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence. Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. Whereas Law Number 1 of 1974 concerning Marriage, which in Article 1 regulates the definition of marriage is a physical and spiritual bond, between a man and a woman to build a household based on the Almighty God. Article 30, regulates that the Obligation of husband and wife is to be faithful to each other, love, help. In this Marriage Law it is regulated regarding who becomes a biological child, as well as joint property, including how to continue its ownership or inheritance to children. If this Law is obeyed, it can prevent and eliminate Domestic Violence, unfortunately what happens in society Domestic Violence (KDRT) is increasingly rampant, precisely with increasingly complex modus operandi and causing increasingly terrible consequences. The principle of non-discrimination is in line with the recognition of human rights, therefore it is very appropriate if the Indonesian Government by enacting Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), in Article 1 states the definition of discrimination against women and all its consequences if discrimination against women occurs. Basically work is only for adults, while children, namely people under the age of 18, are obliged to seek knowledge and play. However, due to the economic limitations of the family, there are some children who have to work. CHAPTER I GENERAL PROVISIONS Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by:

Article 53

Article 20

Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payment or benefits, so as to obtain consent from the person holding control over that other person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in the person being exploited. 7. Article 4

The purpose of establishing this Regional Regulation is to provide protection and services to women and children victims of violence based on gender and the best interests of the child occurring in the household and/or public. As well as to guarantee the fulfillment of children's rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination, for the realization of quality Indonesian children with noble character and prosperity.

From the provisions of the legislation mentioned above, we can understand how great the attention of the Central Government is to protect its citizens who are in an unpleasant position, namely when becoming victims of violence, but in reality legal processes are still few that are carried out for victims of violence which are increasingly numerous and complex in their problems today. In addition, it turns out that the verdicts of District Court judges, there are still many that are far from the demands of community justice, including families and victims of violence. Hopefully with the enactment of this Perda on the Protection of Women and Children Victims of Violence, in Musi Rawas Regency in particular, the handling, and rehabilitation and reintegration can be carried out well, and the process of preventing violence against women and children becomes smoother, so that it becomes less and eventually there is no more violence against women and children. Amen.

In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out. As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity and dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever should not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children, is emphasized by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to deepen the provisions of articles 77 to article 90, which already provide quite severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this perda for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment

is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295 which is 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law is quite severe in establishing criminal threats and fines as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe punishment threats or sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so it is still far from reality, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the demands and verdicts of judges are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays KDRT is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of KDRT in Musi Rawas Regency at the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency, an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency has been established, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/ KPTS/ KPP/2015 namely

concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) becomes a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is KDRT or other violence that befalls women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, but the existence of P2TP2A is not widely known by the community.

CHAPTER III

I. GENERAL

The National Objective of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph states that it includes: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all of Indonesia's homeland, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila, and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal rule on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the right of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence. ELUCIDATION OF REGIONAL REGULATION OF MUSI RAWAS REGENCY NUMBER 4. YEAR 2017 CONCERNING

PROTECTION OF WOMEN AND CHILDREN VICTIMS OF VIOLENCE

I. GENERAL

The National Objective of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph states that it includes: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all of Indonesia's homeland, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila, and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

The principles of this Perda are the principles contained in previous laws and regulations, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, is actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal rule on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government. Also in, Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially regulates that every person, of course both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the right of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence. Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. Whereas Law Number 1 of 1974 concerning Marriage, which in Article 1 regulates the definition of marriage is a physical and spiritual bond, between a man and a woman to build a household based on the Almighty God. Article 30, regulates that the Obligation of husband and wife is to be faithful to each other, love, help. In this Marriage Law it is regulated regarding who becomes a biological child, as well as joint property, including how to continue its ownership or inheritance to children. If this Law is obeyed, it can prevent and eliminate Domestic Violence, unfortunately what happens in society Domestic Violence (KDRT) is increasingly rampant, precisely with increasingly complex modus operandi and causing increasingly terrible consequences. The principle of non-discrimination is in line with the recognition of human rights, therefore it is very appropriate if the Indonesian Government by enacting Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), in Article 1 states the definition of discrimination against women and all its consequences if discrimination against women occurs. Basically work is only for adults, while children, namely people under the age of 18, are obliged to seek knowledge and play. However, due to the economic limitations of the family, there are some children who have to work. Therefore Law Number 20 of 1999, concerning the Minimum Age Limit for Children to be able to work by providing provisions that parents and employers should pay attention to the provisions of this Law, so that even though children are forced to work, they do not lose their youth and can still go to school to guarantee their future. Children who are forced to work are found in all regions, both in urban and rural areas.

Article 4

The purpose of establishing this Regional Regulation is to provide protection and services to women and children victims of violence based on gender and the best interests of the child occurring in the household and/or public. As well as to guarantee the fulfillment of children's rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination, for the realization of quality Indonesian children with noble character and prosperity.

Article 33

Specific protection for children who are victims of unrest, victims of disasters, and children in armed conflict situations as referred to in Article 30 letter b, letter c, and letter d, is implemented through:

a. fulfillment of basic needs consisting of food, clothing, housing, education, health, learning and recreation, security guarantees, and equal treatment; and

b. fulfillment of special needs for children with disabilities and children experiencing psychosocial disorders.

In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out. As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity and dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever should not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children, is emphasized by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to deepen the provisions of articles 77 to article 90, which already provide quite severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this perda for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment

is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295 which is 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law is quite severe in establishing criminal threats and fines as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe punishment threats or sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so it is still far from reality, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the demands and verdicts of judges are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays KDRT is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of KDRT in Musi Rawas Regency at the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency, an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency has been established, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/ KPTS/ KPP/2015 namely

concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) becomes a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is KDRT or other violence that befalls women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, but the existence of P2TP2A is not widely known by the community.

CHAPTER I GENERAL PROVISIONS Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by:

1 . Regency is Musi Rawas Regency; 2. Regency Government is the Government of Musi Rawas Regency; 3. Regent is the Regent of Musi Rawas. 4. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or deprivation of liberty unlawfully within the scope of the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6.

Article 42

(1) Special protection for child victims of abuse and neglect as referred to in Article 30 is carried out through supervision, prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation by the government and society.

(2) Every person is prohibited from placing, allowing, involving, ordering to involve children in situations of abuse and neglect as referred to in paragraph (1).

Article 37

(1) Special protection for children who are exploited economically and/or sexually as referred to in Article 30 is the obligation and responsibility of the government and society.

(2) Special protection for children who are exploited as referred to in paragraph (1) is carried out through:

a. Dissemination and/or socialization of statutory provisions related to the protection of children who are exploited economically and/or sexually;

b. monitoring, reporting, and imposition of sanctions; and

c. involvement of various government agencies, companies, labor unions, non-governmental organizations, and society in the elimination of economic and/or sexual exploitation of children.

(3) Every person is prohibited from placing, allowing, committing, ordering to commit, or participating in the exploitation of children as referred to in paragraph (1).

Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payment or benefits, so as to obtain consent from the person holding control over that other person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in the person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or can result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that results in pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that results in fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse in an unnatural or unwanted manner, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women facing the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under 18 years of age, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in a direct line upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or stepfather and/or stepmother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises parental authority as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental obstacles that interfere with their growth and development naturally. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of the adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because their parents or one of their parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop children in accordance with their religion and abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Child's rights are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, society, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in conflict with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are economically and/or sexually exploited, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substance abuse (drugs), children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of mistreatment and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to the victim when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against the victim will, is, or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for strengthening and self-recovery of victims of violence. 33. Assistance is all actions in the form of counseling, psychological therapy, advocacy, and spiritual guidance, for strengthening victims of domestic violence to resolve the problems they face. 34. Integrated Service Center for Women and Children Empowerment (P2TP2A) hereinafter abbreviated as P2TP2A is an institution providing services to victims of violence, based in hospitals, managed jointly in the form of medical services (including medico-legal), psycho-social and legal services. 35. Cooperation is a systematic and integrated way among recovery implementers in providing services to recover victims of domestic violence. 36. Safe house is a temporary residence used to provide protection to victims in accordance with determined operational standards. 37.

CHAPTER IV IMPLEMENTATION OF PROTECTION Part One Institutions

Article 10

(1) For the implementation of protection for women and children, the Regency Government is obliged to provide services for victims in the form of:

a. establishing and facilitating the operation of integrated service institutions for victims involving community elements; and

b. encouraging community awareness of the importance of protection for victims.

(2). The Regency Government in carrying out its obligations as referred to in paragraph (1), must pay attention to the rights and obligations of parents, guardians, husbands or other persons legally responsible for the victim.

(3). The implementation of Protection Institutions for victims is carried out in an integrated manner within the P2TP2A framework.

(4) Further provisions regarding P2TP2A are regulated in a Regent Regulation.

Part Five Specific Protection

Article 30

The government and other state institutions are obliged and responsible to provide specific protection to children in emergency situations, children in conflict with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substance abuse (napza), children who are victims of kidnapping, sale and trafficking, children who are victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children who are victims of maltreatment and neglect.

Article 25

Children inside and in the school environment must be protected from acts of violence committed by teachers, school administrators or their friends in the school concerned, or other educational institutions.

Article 20

The state, government, family, and parents are obliged to provide the widest possible opportunity for children to obtain education.

CHAPTER VIII ROLE OF THE COMMUNITY Article 58

(1) The community has the right to obtain the widest possible opportunity to participate in the protection of women and children.

(2) The role of the community as referred to in paragraph (1) is carried out by individuals, child protection institutions, social community institutions, non-governmental organizations, educational institutions, religious institutions, business entities, and mass media.

CHAPTER IX

CRIMINAL PROVISIONS

Article 61

Every person who intentionally fails to provide protection to women and children resulting in:

a. the occurrence of violence;

b. allowing the occurrence of violence; and/or

c. failure to report and failure to provide protection to victims, shall be subject to sanctions in accordance with the provisions of laws and regulations.

CHAPTER X CLOSING PROVISIONS Article 62

This Regional Regulation shall come into force on the date of promulgation.

In order that everyone may know of it, the promulgation of this Regional Regulation is ordered by placing it in the Regional Gazette of Musi Rawas Regency.

In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out. As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity and dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever should not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children, is emphasized by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to deepen the provisions of articles 77 to article 90, which already provide quite severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this perda for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment

is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295 which is 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law is quite severe in establishing criminal threats and fines as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe punishment threats or sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so it is still far from reality, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the demands and verdicts of judges are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays KDRT is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of KDRT in Musi Rawas Regency at the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency, an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency has been established, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/ KPTS/ KPP/2015 namely

concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Children (P2TP2A) becomes a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is KDRT or other violence that befalls women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, but the existence of P2TP2A is not widely known by the community.

Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payment or benefits, so as to obtain consent from the person holding control over that other person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in the person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or can result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that results in pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that results in fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or stepfather and/or stepmother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises parental authority as a parent over a child. 18. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. Examples related to this perda for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment

is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment of a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of a maximum of Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and a minimum of Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295 which is 12 years. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the demands and verdicts of judges are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payment or benefits, so as to obtain consent from the person holding control over that other person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in the person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or can result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that results in pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that results in fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse in an unnatural or unwanted manner, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women facing the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under 18 years of age, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in a direct line upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or stepfather and/or stepmother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises parental authority as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental obstacles that interfere with their growth and development naturally. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of the adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because their parents or one of their parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop children in accordance with their religion and abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Child's rights are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, society, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in conflict with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are economically and/or sexually exploited, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substance abuse (drugs), children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of mistreatment and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to the victim when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against the victim will, is, or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for strengthening and self-recovery of victims of violence. 33. Assistance is all actions in the form of counseling, psychological therapy, advocacy, and spiritual guidance, for strengthening victims of domestic violence to resolve the problems they face. 34. Integrated Service Center for Women and Children Empowerment (P2TP2A) hereinafter abbreviated as P2TP2A is an institution providing services to victims of violence, based in hospitals, managed jointly in the form of medical services (including medico-legal), psycho-social and legal services. 35. Cooperation is a systematic and integrated way among recovery implementers in providing services to recover victims of domestic violence. 36. Safe house is a temporary residence used to provide protection to victims in accordance with determined operational standards. 37.

Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of KDRT, in essence is to realize a sakinah, mawadah, and warokhmah household, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of KDRT, (c) prosecuting perpetrators of KDRT and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. In order for us to better understand the prohibition of KDRT, a brief description of important matters from Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning KDRT will be outlined as follows:

Types of KDRT, include:

a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) falling ill, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of helplessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, who resides within the household, (2) forced sexual relations against one person within the household with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household, whereas according to the law applicable to him or because of an agreement or contract he is obliged to provide life, care, or

maintenance to that person or child, (2) resulting in economic dependence by limiting and/or prohibiting to work properly inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. The rights of KDRT victims are to obtain:
